function_v0.doc:
Cancel a pending operation. `canceller` must hold `CANCELLER` or `GUARDIAN`.

Takes the operation itself rather than its id, as [`Self::execute`] does, and rebuilds the
id from it. The id is a hash, so a canceller holding only that cannot be told apart from one
cancelling the owner's recovery path \xe2\x80\x94 and the alternative, a stored per-id marker, buys
that distinction with persistent state, a TTL to size, and a cleanup path to get right.
Rebuilding is free and makes the caller name what it is killing.
function_v0.name: cancel

function_v0.doc:
Execute a Ready operation, invoking `target.function(args)` authorized as this contract.
`executor` must authorize the call and hold the `EXECUTOR` role \xe2\x80\x94 the role is enforced on
every execution, there is no anonymous path. A deployment that wants permissionless
execution grants `EXECUTOR` to a designated relayer address explicitly. Returns the
target's result.
function_v0.name: execute

function_v0.doc:
Execute a Ready `upgrade(new_wasm_hash)` self-operation scheduled under `salt`. Address and
storage are preserved. `executor` must hold `EXECUTOR`.

The salt matters here too: rolling back to a wasm hash this contract has run before is a
normal recovery step, and a fixed salt made it permanently unschedulable.
function_v0.name: upgrade

function_v0.doc:
Schedule an admin `(target, function, args)` call on the timelock; returns its operation id.
The delay is derived from the method's [`Tier`] via [`classify`] \xe2\x80\x94 the caller does not choose
it, so a Sensitive change (upgrade, admin/ownership, live-pool risk) always carries the
elevated floor.

`proposer` must hold the role that owns the derived tier: `ADL` for `apply_adl`,
`FEE_DISTRIBUTOR` for `set_fee_merkle_root`, and `PROPOSER` for the governance tiers (see
[`ensure_can_schedule`]). The scoped keys reach their own tier and nothing else.
function_v0.name: schedule

function_v0.doc: The ADL-tier delay in ledgers. Zero selects [`Self::execute_adl`]; a non-zero value selects\nthe ordinary schedule/execute/cancel lifecycle.
function_v0.name: adl_delay

function_v0.doc:
Execute a Ready `grant_role(account, role)` self-operation scheduled under `salt`.
`executor` must hold `EXECUTOR`, exactly as on [`Self::execute_self`].

The salt is a parameter rather than a fixed zero because an executed id is `Done` forever \xe2\x80\x94
the timelock never returns one to `Unset`, and `cancel` refuses a `Done` entry \xe2\x80\x94 so a
hardcoded salt made this entry point single-use per `(function, account, role)`. Granting a
role, revoking it, and later restoring it is ordinary operations work, and the third step
reverted permanently with an error that read as a timelock bug.
function_v0.name: grant_role

function_v0.doc:
Immediately execute `target.apply_adl(args)` through governance.

ADL names a live candidate and defaults to a zero-ledger delay. A zero-delay operational
action is not a timelocked governance proposal, so this path deliberately creates no
[`Operation`], salt or pending state: the scoped backend is authorized here and the target
call either succeeds in this invocation or rolls back with it.

`operator` must hold the dedicated `ADL` role. The function is hard-coded rather than
supplied by the caller, so this capability reaches only `apply_adl`. A non-zero ADL delay
disables this gateway; delayed ADL operations use the ordinary schedule/execute/cancel
lifecycle.
function_v0.name: execute_adl

function_v0.doc: Execute a Ready `revoke_role(account, role)` self-operation scheduled under `salt`.\n`executor` must hold `EXECUTOR`. See [`Self::grant_role`] for why the salt is a parameter.
function_v0.name: revoke_role

function_v0.doc:
Execute a Ready Sensitive operation whose target is this governance contract. Self-calls
cannot use [`Self::execute`] because Soroban rejects governance -> governance re-entry, so
this path consumes the operation with OZ's `set_execute_operation` and dispatches the
allowlisted action internally: `upgrade`, `grant_role`, `revoke_role`, or one of the five
per-tier `set_*_delay` retunes. Each retune takes one `u32` of ledgers, bounded by
[`MAX_DELAY_LEDGERS`] as at construction, and is the only way to move that delay after
deploy \xe2\x80\x94 the values live in storage, so a later `upgrade` alone cannot reach them.

Like [`Self::execute`], `executor` must authorize the call and hold the `EXECUTOR` role:
scheduling and the Sensitive delay decide *what* can run and *when*, the executor decides
the moment it lands, and a guardian can cancel while it is pending.
function_v0.name: execute_self

function_v0.doc:
Initialize governance: `admin` becomes owner + access-control admin and holds all seven
operational roles. One delay per [`Tier`], all in ledgers, each independent of the others and
each retunable afterwards by its own self-operation. `DEFAULT_SENSITIVE_DELAY_LEDGERS`,
[`DEFAULT_ADL_DELAY_LEDGERS`] and [`DEFAULT_FEE_DISTRIBUTION_DELAY_LEDGERS`] are the
recommended mainnet values; a dev/testnet deploy passes `0` for all five, which is the only
way to turn the timelock off \xe2\x80\x94 no tier's value silently zeroes another.

Handing `ADL` / `FEE_DISTRIBUTOR` to the off-chain services is a `grant_role`
self-operation, after which the admin should drop its own copies.

OZ's own `min_delay` is pinned to `0` and left there. It exists to stop a caller passing
`schedule_operation` a delay under the configured floor, and here no caller ever passes one:
[`Self::schedule`] is the only path in and derives the delay from the method's tier. Leaving
the library floor armed would only mean it silently overrode four of our five tier
function_v0.name: __constructor

function_v0.doc:
Immediately invoke a **creation-only** admin call \xe2\x80\x94 `create_pool`, `initialize_pool`,
`approve_pool`, `configure` \xe2\x80\x94 authorized as this contract, bypassing the timelock. `deployer`
must hold `DEPLOYER`, and the method must classify as [`Tier::Deployer`] (else
`NotADeployerOperation`). These methods reject an already-configured target; LockYield also
tombstones every `revoke_pool`, so `approve_pool` cannot resurrect it. Restoring that pool
requires the separate, Sensitive `reapprove_pool` operation. Thus this fast path can bring
up a new pool but can never retune or restore a live one \xe2\x80\x94 that (and registering a margin
asset) stays on the Sensitive setters, reachable only through `schedule` + the delay.
Returns the target's result.
function_v0.name: deployer_call

function_v0.doc: The Deployer tier's delay, in ledgers \xe2\x80\x94 for a creation-only op that is *scheduled* rather\nthan driven through the immediate [`Self::deployer_call`].
function_v0.name: deployer_delay

function_v0.doc:
Emergency brake: immediately (bypassing the timelock) pause `target` by invoking
`target.set_paused(true)` authorized as this contract. `guardian` must hold `GUARDIAN`. The
target must be a contract whose admin is this governance and that exposes `set_paused(bool)`.

**Pause only.** `paused == false` is rejected (`GuardianCanOnlyPause`); unpausing is a
`Tier::Standard` `set_paused(false)` through `schedule`. The brake is deliberately
one-directional: halting during an incident cannot wait for a delay, but restarting is a
judgement call that should be visible as a pending operation and cancellable by anyone
holding `CANCELLER` or `GUARDIAN`. Forwarding the flag let a single compromised guardian key
clear a pause the instant it was set \xe2\x80\x94 reopening the exploit window with nothing scheduled
to cancel, while honest governance had to wait out the full delay to re-pause.

The `paused` argument survives the restriction rather than being dropped so the call shape
(and every runbook and script built on it) stays put,
function_v0.name: guardian_pause

function_v0.doc: The [`Tier`] a method schedules at \xe2\x80\x94 lets ops tell ahead of time whether a call is an instant\n`deployer_call`, a min-delay `schedule`, or a Sensitive-floor `schedule`.
function_v0.name: operation_tier

function_v0.name: standard_delay

function_v0.name: sensitive_delay

function_v0.doc: The delay a fee-distribution-tier op (`set_fee_merkle_root`) schedules at (ledgers).
function_v0.name: fee_distribution_delay

function_v0.doc:
Schedule a grant or revoke of `role` on `account` that no canceller or guardian can veto.
Owner-gated; returns the operation id. Execute it with `execute_self` once the Sensitive
delay has run, passing the same arguments and this path's reserved salt (readable from the
emitted operation, or rebuilt as 32 `0xFF` bytes).

The recovery lever, and the only one: role administration is otherwise a Sensitive
self-operation, and `cancel` accepts any pending operation from any canceller or guardian \xe2\x80\x94
so a compromised holder vetoes its own removal indefinitely, and a compromised guardian
keeps the engine paused on top of that. Forbidding cancellation of *every* `revoke_role`
would swap that deadlock for a worse one: a compromised proposer could then strip every
other holder unopposed, and since granting a role is itself a proposer-scheduled operation,
nothing could put them back.

Timelocked like any other Sensitive change \xe2\x80\x94 the owner gets notice, not immediacy \xe2\x80\x94 and
scoped to role changes alone.
